blocks.title: How often each candidate appears just after Bob gets a message

scenes.caption: After 1 message: Alice and hundreds of strangers each appear once. No signal yet.
After 3 messages: Alice has appeared every time; the best stranger only twice.
After 5 messages: Alice 5, best stranger 2. The paper's theoretical and simulation-based models gave as few as 5 messages.
After 8 messages: the server has linked the sealed sender without ever seeing a sender field.

blocks.md: **Mitigations.** The paper proposes protocol changes that it proves secure for one-sided anonymity "over any sequence of messages", the simplest reusing much of sealed sender's existing machinery at small extra cost. More generally, traffic padding, delaying or batching receipts, and mixing networks all raise the cost. Signal's own 2018 post already said that resistance to "traffic correlation via timing attacks and IP addresses" was ongoing work. Other metadata, such as group membership, needs separate cryptography: Signal's private group system (lesson 13) keeps member lists encrypted on the server.
Hiding a field is not hiding a pattern. Any metadata defence must be judged over many messages and against an observer who sees timing, sizes and automatic replies, not one message at a time.

blocks.question: Sealed sender hides the sender of each message. Why could the server still link Alice and Bob?
options: Repeated timing correlation: Bob's automatic delivery receipts go to Alice just after each message reaches Bob
Sealed sender only works over Wi-Fi
blocks.explain: The server never decrypts anything. It counts who receives something right after Bob does; Alice appears every time, strangers rarely. Delivery receipts make the pattern sharper.

blocks.question: Which change would most directly weaken the statistical disclosure attack described here?
options: Delaying, batching or padding automatic receipts so they stop marking a tight time window
blocks.explain: The attack lives on timing. Breaking the tight link between delivery and reply (or adopting the paper's provably secure protocol changes) is what helps; stronger ciphers and key rotation do not touch metadata.

lessons.title: Group chats: pairwise fan-out, sender keys, and who decides membership

blocks.md:
A group of n people could reuse what we have: the sender encrypts each message separately over each pairwise Double Ratchet session (**client fan-out**). That is simple and keeps every pairwise property, but costs n - 1 encryptions and uploads per message.

**Sender keys** cut that cost. WhatsApp's encryption whitepaper (updated 30 October 2026) describes them: the first time a member sends to a group, they generate a random 32-byte chain key and a signature key pair, and send this "Sender Key" to each member over the pairwise sessions. After that, each message key comes from a hash ratchet on the chain key, the message is encrypted once and signed, and "the server ... does server-side fan-out to all group participants". The hash ratchet gives forward secrecy, and "whenever a group member leaves, all group participants clear their Sender Key and start over".

blocks.title: Encryptions the sender performs per message in a group of 50

scenes.caption: Client fan-out: one encryption per other member, 49 in all, each over a pairwise ratchet.
Sender keys: one encryption and one signature; the server copies the ciphertext. The 49 pairwise sends happen only when a sender key is (re)distributed.

blocks.md:
The cost of the shortcut is post-compromise security. A sender key is only a symmetric hash ratchet: whoever steals it can follow that sender's chain until the key is replaced, which happens when membership changes, not when time passes. Paul Rösler, Christian Mainka and Jörg Schwenk ("More is Less", EuroS&P 2018) analysed Signal, WhatsApp and Threema groups and found that "the groups' closeness", meaning members' control over who is in the group, was "not end-to-end protected", and that strong properties of one-to-one Signal "do not hold for its group communication".

The membership problem is the dangerous one. If the *server* decides who is in the group, clients will happily hand the next sender key to whoever the server lists.

blocks.caption: Vulnerable and fixed membership handling. The fix accepts membership changes only when signed by an identity the members already trust. Toy, not for production.

blocks.code:
vulnerable sends key to: ['ana', 'bob', 'cy', 'mallory']
checked client:
  rejected unsigned change: add:mallory
  sends key to: ['ana', 'bob', 'cy', 'di']
blocks.caption: Output when run. The server could list Mallory but cannot forge an admin's signature.

blocks.md: Why the fix works: the decision "who receives keys" is bound to a key held only by group members, so the server is demoted to a courier. Real systems do this in different ways. Signal's **private group system** ([paper](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1416) by Melissa Chase and Greg Zaverucha of Microsoft Research with Trevor Perrin, ACM CCS 2020) stores the member list on the server as encrypted entries, and members prove with anonymous credentials that they belong, so the server neither sees nor controls the list. MLS (next two lessons) makes every membership change a signed, confirmed step of the group key schedule.

Showing "Mallory joined" in the timeline is not a fix. In large groups nobody reads membership events, as the Matrix researchers point out in lesson 18. Membership must be cryptographically authorised, or at least require explicit acceptance before keys are sent.

blocks.question: What does a stolen sender key let an attacker do?
options: Read that member's future group messages until the sender key is replaced, typically at the next membership change
blocks.explain: The hash ratchet gives forward secrecy, so past keys are safe. But without a DH ratchet there is no healing; the chain continues until the group resets sender keys, which WhatsApp does when a member leaves.

blocks.question: In the vulnerable toy, which party really controls the group's confidentiality?
options: The server, because clients send keys to whatever member list it provides
blocks.explain: Whoever decides the recipient list of the sender key decides who can read. If that list is unauthenticated server data, the server holds the power E2EE was meant to remove.

lessons.title: MLS ratchet trees: updating a big group in log n steps

blocks.md:
**MLS** (Messaging Layer Security), RFC 9420 (July 2023), is the IETF's standard for group key agreement. Its abstract promises "efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS) for groups in size ranging from two to thousands". The idea at its core was proposed in 2018 by Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Richard Barnes and Eric Rescorla as **TreeKEM**: tree plus KEM (key encapsulation mechanism).

Arrange the members as leaves of a binary tree. Every node has an **HPKE** key pair (Hybrid Public Key Encryption, [RFC 9180](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9180): a public-key encryption scheme built from a KEM, a KDF and an AEAD). Each member knows the private keys of the nodes on the path from its own leaf to the root. This **tree invariant**, says the RFC, "makes it possible to encrypt to all group members except one, with a number of ciphertexts that is logarithmic in the number of group members".

blocks.title: Member A updates: fresh secrets up the path, one ciphertext per level

scenes.caption: Eight members A to H. Each knows the private keys on its own leaf-to-root path (A knows A, AB, ABCD and the root).
A picks a random path_secret[0] for node AB and derives the next ones by hashing: path_secret[n] = DeriveSecret(path_secret[n-1], "path").
A encrypts each path secret to the sibling subtree (the copath): AB's to B, ABCD's to CD, the root's to EFGH. Three ciphertexts for seven members.
Each member decrypts the one ciphertext addressed to a node it knows, then hashes upward to the same root secret. A's old keys are gone: healing for the whole group.

blocks.title: A toy TreeKEM commit with real X25519 and AES-GCM
blocks.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey as X
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.hashes import SHA256
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
def derive(secret, label):                 # stands in for MLS DeriveSecret
    return HKDF(SHA256(), 32, None, label).derive(secret)
def keypair(path_secret):                  # node key pair from a path secret
    return X.from_private_bytes(derive(derive(path_secret, b"node"), b"kp"))
def seal(pub, msg):                        # toy HPKE: ephemeral DH + AEAD
    e = X.generate(); k = derive(e.exchange(pub), b"seal")
    return e.public_key(), AESGCM(k).encrypt(b"\0" * 12, msg, None)
def open_(priv, box):
    k = derive(priv.exchange(box[0]), b"seal")
    return AESGCM(k).decrypt(b"\0" * 12, box[1], None)
# 8 members A..H. tree[level][i]: level 0 = leaves, level 3 = root
tree = [[keypair(os.urandom(32)) for _ in range(8 >> lv)] for lv in range(4)]
# A (leaf 0) commits: fresh secrets up its direct path, one box per level
ps = [os.urandom(32)]                      # path_secret[0], for level 1
for _ in range(2):
    ps.append(derive(ps[-1], b"path"))     # path_secret[n] from [n-1]
boxes = [seal(tree[lv][1].public_key(), ps[lv]) for lv in range(3)]
for lv in range(3):                        # A now owns the new node keys
    tree[lv + 1][0] = keypair(ps[lv])
print("ciphertexts sent:", len(boxes), "for 7 other members")
# Each member opens the box for the copath node it sits under, then hashes up
roots = {}
for m in range(1, 8):
    lv = m.bit_length() - 1                # B:0, C-D:1, E-H:2
    s = open_(tree[lv][m >> lv], boxes[lv])
    for _ in range(lv, 2):
        s = derive(s, b"path")
    roots["ABCDEFGH"[m]] = s
print("everyone has A's root secret:", set(roots.values()) == {ps[2]})

scenes.caption: Helpers: a DeriveSecret stand-in (HKDF), a node key pair derived from a path secret, and a toy HPKE (ephemeral X25519 plus AES-GCM).
A tree of 8 leaves and 7 parent nodes, each with a key pair.
A samples path_secret[0] and hashes it twice, giving secrets for AB, ABCD and the root.
One sealed box per level, each to the sibling node: leaf B, node CD, node EFGH. A replaces its path keys.
Each member opens the box at its level and hashes up the remaining levels. All seven reach A's new root secret.
scenes.output: everyone has A's root secret: True

blocks.code:
ciphertexts sent: 3 for 7 other members
everyone has A's root secret: True
blocks.caption: Real output. Toy, not for production: real MLS uses RFC 9180 HPKE, a full key schedule, signatures, tree hashes and blank-node handling.

blocks.md:
**Removal and blanks.** To remove a member, the committer blanks that member's leaf and the nodes above it, then sends a fresh path that the removed member cannot decrypt, because every ciphertext goes to a node whose private key the removed member never held. Blank nodes are skipped by encrypting to their **resolution** (the non-blank nodes below them), so a tree full of departures costs more ciphertexts until members update again.

In a balanced tree of n members an update costs about log2(n) ciphertexts: 3 for 8, 10 for 1024. Pairwise fan-out needs n - 1.

A ratchet tree lets any member inject fresh randomness for the whole group with a logarithmic number of encryptions. That gives groups the post-compromise security that sender keys lack, at a cost that scales to thousands.

blocks.question: In an 8-member MLS tree, member A commits an update. To which node does A encrypt the new root's path secret?
options: To every leaf E, F, G and H separately
To node EFGH, whose private key exactly E, F, G and H hold
blocks.explain: The root's secret goes to the copath node on that level, EFGH. One ciphertext covers four members because they all know EFGH's private key by the tree invariant.

blocks.question: Why can a removed member not read the group after the removing commit?
options: Every new path secret is encrypted only to nodes whose private keys the removed member never held, since their leaf and path were blanked
blocks.explain: The commit rebuilds the path with fresh secrets and encrypts them to the remaining copath nodes. The removed member knows only old, blanked keys.

lessons.title: MLS in practice: proposals, commits, epochs and the two services

blocks.md:
An MLS group moves through **epochs**. Each epoch has one shared **epoch secret**, from which the key schedule derives message encryption keys, an exporter for applications, and more. To change anything, a member sends **Proposals** (Add, Remove, Update) and then a **Commit** that applies a list of proposals and usually carries a fresh UpdatePath like the one in lesson 14. Everyone who processes the Commit moves to the next epoch.

New members join from a **KeyPackage**, a signed bundle of their HPKE key and credential that they uploaded earlier, playing the role of X3DH prekeys. The committer sends them a **Welcome** message with the secrets they need. Each member also keeps a **GroupContext** with the epoch number, a hash of the tree and a hash of the transcript of commits, which binds the keys to the exact group state.

blocks.title: Alice adds Bob and Charlie, then Bob updates

scenes.caption: Bob and Charlie publish KeyPackages to the Delivery Service ahead of time, as with prekeys.
Alice fetches Bob's KeyPackage, checks its credential with the Authentication Service's rules, and commits an Add. Epoch 1 begins.
Adding Charlie: the Commit goes to existing members, the Welcome to Charlie. All three are in epoch 2.
Bob commits an Update with a fresh path. Any key stolen from Bob before epoch 3 no longer opens new messages.

blocks.md:
**Two services, two kinds of trust.** RFC 9750 (April 2025), the MLS architecture, splits the infrastructure in two:

- The **Authentication Service** (AS) attests "bindings between application-meaningful identifiers and the public key material". It is the key directory of MLS, and RFC 9750 warns that "the compromise of the AS could allow an adversary to, among other things, impersonate group members", recommending HSMs (hardware security modules) for its root keys. Key transparency (lesson 11) is one way to keep it honest.
- The **Delivery Service** (DS) stores KeyPackages and routes messages. It is trusted for availability, not confidentiality: it can drop or delay messages and see metadata, but cannot read content or forge commits.

When handshake messages are encrypted, RFC 9750 notes that "any access control policies must be applied at the client", consistently on every client.

**Checking you share one group.** Every epoch also yields an **epoch_authenticator**. RFC 9420: if a member is impersonated by an active attacker, "the epoch_authenticator computed by their client will differ from those computed by the other group members". Comparing it out of band is a group-sized safety number, valid only for the current epoch.

**Cipher suites.** The mandatory one is MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_AES128GCM_SHA256_Ed25519: X25519 for HPKE, AES-128-GCM, HKDF over SHA-256 and Ed25519 signatures. All are classical; an IETF draft adds ML-KEM and hybrid suites, and NIST IR 8547 disallows ECC after 2035, so plan the move.

**Deployment.** In March 2025 the GSMA (the mobile operators' industry body) announced RCS (Rich Communication Services) Universal Profile 3.0, whose [new specifications](https://www.gsma.com/newsroom/article/rcs-encryption-a-leap-towards-secure-and-interoperable-messaging/) "define how to apply MLS within the context of RCS", aiming at interoperable E2EE between messaging apps from different vendors.

MLS replaces ad hoc group logic with one rule: every change to membership or keys is a signed Commit that moves the whole group to a new epoch with a new secret. The AS must be kept honest; the DS only needs to deliver.

blocks.question: In MLS, which service is trusted with identity, and what happens if it is compromised?
options: The Authentication Service; an attacker could issue credentials and impersonate members
The Delivery Service; messages get delayed
Neither; MLS needs no identity service
The Delivery Service; content can be read
blocks.explain: RFC 9750 says a compromised AS can generate and sign new credentials and impersonate group members. The DS is trusted only for delivery and cannot read content.

blocks.question: A member lost their phone, which held their MLS state. What should happen in the group?
options: Nothing; the epoch secret expires daily
Remove that leaf (or have the member re-join and update) in a new Commit so later epochs use secrets the lost device cannot derive
Ask the DS to delete old messages
blocks.explain: The lost device knows the current epoch's secrets and its path keys. A Commit that removes or replaces its leaf, with a fresh path, gives post-compromise security; earlier epochs stay protected by forward secrecy once keys are deleted.

lessons.title: Many devices per person: Sesame, fan-out and linked-device phishing

blocks.md:
People use a phone, a laptop and a tablet. Each device has its own keys, so "send to Bob" really means "send to each of Bob's devices, and to my own other devices so they show what I sent". Signal's **Sesame** spec (revision 2, 2017) manages these sessions. It notes that Alice and Bob "might each have several devices" and "might add and remove devices", and supports either per-user identity keys (all of a user's devices share one key pair) or per-device identity keys. The server "stores the current record of all users and devices": the **device list** is server data.

WhatsApp's multi-device design (July 2021) uses **client fan-out**: the sending client encrypts "N number of times to N number of different devices", each over its own pairwise session, with up to four companion devices besides the phone. Unlike Sesame's bare server record, the primary phone signs WhatsApp's device list and each companion's key, and security codes cover all devices, so a server cannot silently add a reader.

blocks.title: Linked-device phishing: no exploit, just one QR scan

scenes.caption: The attacker starts the legitimate 'link a new device' flow on their own machine and gets a linking URI (rendered as a QR code).
The QR code is dressed up as a group invite or a security alert and sent to the victim.
The victim scans it with the messaging app, which treats it as a request to link a device and approves.
From now on the server lists the attacker's device as one of the victim's, and every sender fans out a copy to it.
Defence: the victim checks Settings, Linked devices, removes the unknown one, and its sessions stop receiving copies.

blocks.md: **Case: Russia-aligned actors against Signal (February 2025).** Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reported that the "most novel and widely used technique" was abuse of the "linked devices" feature with malicious QR codes, so that "future messages will be delivered synchronously to both the victim and the threat actor in real-time" without full device compromise. One cluster, UNC5792, altered Signal group-invite pages so that their redirect pointed at the device-linking URI instead of a group. APT44 (APT: advanced persistent threat; also called Sandworm, which governments attribute to the GRU's Main Centre for Special Technologies, unit 74455) worked to link Signal accounts on devices captured on the battlefield to actor infrastructure. GTIG called device linking "a low-signature form of initial access" with a risk of going unnoticed for long periods, and said new Signal releases contained hardened features against these campaigns.

Every linked device is a full reader of future messages. The device list is the multi-device equivalent of a group member list: if it can change without the user noticing, E2EE quietly includes the attacker.

Defender view: teach high-risk users that a QR code from a chat or web page should never be scanned with the messaging app's link-device function; review linked devices regularly; prefer apps that notify on new links and show last-active times (WhatsApp's design shows when each companion was last used). In incident response, ask "which devices are linked?" before assuming malware.

blocks.question: Why does a maliciously linked device not trigger the protocol's cryptographic checks?
options: It uses an old protocol version
The user approved it, so it gets a genuine identity in the user's device list, and senders legitimately encrypt to it
blocks.explain: The cryptography works exactly as designed: the device is enrolled through the real flow. That is why GTIG calls it low-signature; detection depends on the device list being visible and reviewed.

blocks.question: In Sesame's model, who holds the authoritative list of a user's devices?
options: The server, which senders consult before fanning out
blocks.explain: Sesame assumes a server that stores the current record of users and devices. That makes device-list changes a server-side power unless clients authenticate them: WhatsApp has the primary phone sign the device list, and Automatic Device Verification and security codes cover all devices, so the server cannot silently add one.

lessons.title: Backups and cloud copies: the quiet way around E2EE

blocks.md:
Ratchets delete keys so that old messages cannot be decrypted. Backups exist to do the opposite: keep old messages readable after a phone is lost. Whatever protects the backup becomes the real protection for the whole history.

**Apple, standard protection.** Apple's [iCloud data security overview](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102651) says that with standard data protection the backup keys are "secured in Apple data centers", and if you use iCloud Backup and Messages in iCloud, "your backup includes a copy of the Messages in iCloud encryption key". So iMessage is E2EE in transit, but a standard iCloud backup lets Apple (or whoever compels Apple) recover the messages. **Advanced Data Protection** (ADP, optional) makes "iCloud Backup and everything inside it" end-to-end encrypted, "including the Messages in iCloud encryption key".

**The UK case.** In February 2025 the BBC and the Washington Post [reported](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgj54eq4vejo) that the UK Home Office had served Apple a notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 seeking access to encrypted iCloud data; neither confirmed it. Apple's [support page](https://support.apple.com/en-us/122234) "Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection in the United Kingdom to new users" says UK users who had not enabled ADP "will no longer have the option to do so", leaving iCloud Backup, iCloud Drive, Photos, Notes and other categories under standard protection, while "iMessage and FaceTime, remain end-to-end encrypted globally, including in the UK". Apple added: "we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will". The message content stays E2EE on the wire; the backup copy is where access moved.

**WhatsApp (September 2021)** offered [E2EE backups](https://engineering.fb.com/2021/09/10/security/whatsapp-e2ee-backups/) encrypted with a random key that users either keep themselves (a 64-digit key) or protect with a password. With a password, the key lives in an HSM-based **Backup Key Vault** that enforces "password verification attempts" and renders the key "permanently inaccessible after a limited number of unsuccessful attempts".

**Signal (September 2025)** began rolling out opt-in [secure backups](https://signal.org/blog/introducing-secure-backups/) protected by a 64-character recovery key generated on the device and "never shared with Signal's servers"; losing it means losing the backup.

Why the attempt limit matters: people choose short secrets. If the backup key is wrapped under a key derived only from a password or PIN, anyone who copies the wrapped blob can try every guess offline, as fast as their hardware allows. A slow KDF (key derivation function, from crypto-building-blocks) only multiplies the cost per guess. A vault that counts wrong guesses and erases the key turns the same short PIN into a hard limit.

blocks.code:
# Toy backup-key protection, not for production. A 4-digit PIN protects
# a random 32-byte backup key in two different ways.
import hashlib, os, hmac
PIN = b"2580"
salt = os.urandom(16)
slow = lambda pin: hashlib.scrypt(pin, salt=salt, n=2**10, r=8, p=1, dklen=32)

# VULNERABLE: the key is wrapped under a key derived only from the PIN, and
# the wrapped blob sits on a server. Whoever copies the blob guesses offline.
check = hmac.new(slow(PIN), b"check", "sha256").digest()
for guess in range(10_000):
    g = f"{guess:04d}".encode()
    if hmac.new(slow(g), b"check", "sha256").digest() == check:
        print("offline attacker found PIN", g.decode(), "after", guess + 1, "guesses")
        break

# FIXED: a hardware-backed vault releases the key only for the right PIN
# and erases it after a fixed number of wrong tries.
class Vault:
    def __init__(s, pin, key, tries=10):
        s.pin, s.key, s.left = pin, key, tries
    def unlock(s, pin):
        if s.key is None:
            return "key erased"
        if hmac.compare_digest(pin, s.pin):
            return s.key
        s.left -= 1
        if s.left == 0:
            s.key = None
        return "wrong PIN"

v = Vault(PIN, os.urandom(32))
results = [v.unlock(f"{g:04d}".encode()) for g in range(12)]
print("vault answers:", results.count("wrong PIN"), "wrong, then", results[-1])
blocks.caption: Offline guessing against a PIN-wrapped key, and the attempt-limited vault that fixes it (scrypt at 2^10 for speed; at 2^17 all 10,000 PINs still fall, slower). Toy, not for production: a real vault is an HSM or secure element, and the PIN check itself must be protected in transit.

blocks.code:
offline attacker found PIN 2580 after 2581 guesses
vault answers: 10 wrong, then key erased
blocks.caption: Output when run. Even with scrypt the 4-digit space fell in a few seconds on a laptop; the vault allowed 10 guesses in total.

blocks.title: Where the message history can be recovered from

scenes.caption: Messages are E2EE between the phones. So far only the endpoints can read them.
A cloud backup whose key the provider holds: the provider (or a court, or a hacker of it) can decrypt the whole history.
E2EE backup, key wrapped under a short password with no attempt limit: anyone who copies the blob can guess offline.
E2EE backup with a long recovery key held by the user, or a short PIN behind an attempt-limited HSM: the provider stores only ciphertext.

blocks.md: **Backups can leak through the format, too.** The ETH Zürich analysis of Threema (lesson 18) found that Threema Safe compressed backup data before encrypting it, and since an attacker controls part of that data (their own username in the victim's contact list), the compressed size leaked information, as in the CRIME attack on TLS (where the length of compressed, encrypted traffic let an attacker guess secret HTTP headers). Forcing many backups could let an attacker "extract the victim user's long-term key". Threema has since mitigated the issues.
A conversation is only as private as its least protected copy. Ask of every messenger: is the backup on by default, who holds its key, and is a short secret protected by an attempt limit?

blocks.question: Bob's iMessage threads are E2EE, and Bob uses standard iCloud Backup with Messages in iCloud. Who can recover Bob's message history from Apple's servers?
options: Apple, because the backup includes the Messages in iCloud key and Apple holds the backup keys under standard protection
Only someone with Bob's unlocked phone
blocks.explain: Apple's own overview says the backup includes that key and that standard-protection backup keys are held in Apple data centers. Advanced Data Protection changes this by making the backup itself end-to-end encrypted.

blocks.question: A design wraps the backup key with scrypt(PIN) and stores the wrapped key on the provider's server. What is the core weakness?
options: A short PIN can be guessed offline by anyone holding the wrapped key; nothing limits attempts
blocks.explain: A slow KDF only raises the cost per guess; 10,000 PINs is still tiny. An HSM or secure element that counts failures (as in WhatsApp's vault) or a long random key held by the user removes offline guessing.

lessons.title: When protocols broke: Matrix (2022) and Threema (2023)

blocks.md: **Matrix** is an open, federated messaging standard; its flagship client is Element. Encryption uses **Olm** (a pairwise ratchet protocol) and **Megolm** (a sender-key-style group ratchet) on top of **homeservers**, the servers that hold each user's account and room state. In September 2022 Martin Albrecht and Daniel Jones (Royal Holloway), Sofía Celi (Brave) and Benjamin Dowling (Sheffield) published "Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix". Every attack "require[s] cooperation of the homeserver", which is exactly the attacker E2EE is meant to resist. Their summary: Matrix and Element "provided neither authentication nor confidentiality against homeservers that actively attack the protocol".

What broke, by root cause:

- **Server-controlled membership.** Room management messages "are not authenticated", so a malicious homeserver could add a user it controls, and members would share Megolm keys with it. A second variant added an attacker device to a real user's account. Element shows the event, but "in sufficiently big rooms such an event is likely to go unnoticed".
- **Identifier confusion.** Device IDs and key IDs were "used interchangeably", so a homeserver could get a target to verify a cross-signing identity (the key vouching for a user's devices) it controlled: a lack of **domain separation** (one value meaning two things).
- **Unverified key forwarding** and a **protocol confusion** (a Megolm key accepted if merely encrypted, not encrypted over Olm) let an attacker impersonate devices and steer a victim's key backup to an attacker key.
- **IV not under the MAC** in AES-CTR backups: a theoretical IND-CCA break.

Disclosed between May and July 2022, with fixes from 28 September 2022; Matrix treated server-controlled membership as an accepted risk to mitigate later.

blocks.code:
# Toy, not for production: one signature, two meanings (no domain separation).
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey as Ed
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature
alice = Ed.generate()

def vouch_device(device_id, typed):       # "I verified this device"
    return alice.sign((b"device:" if typed else b"") + device_id)

def trusts_identity_key(sig, key_id, typed):   # "I verified this identity key"
    try:
        alice.public_key().verify(sig, (b"identity-key:" if typed else b"") + key_id)
        return True
    except InvalidSignature:
        return False

# A malicious server names a device with the same string as the ID of an
# identity key that the attacker controls, and Alice verifies "the device".
attacker_key_id = b"Q3vX9w...base64"
for typed in (False, True):
    sig = vouch_device(attacker_key_id, typed)
    print("typed labels" if typed else "untyped     ",
          "| device vouch accepted as identity-key vouch:",
          trusts_identity_key(sig, attacker_key_id, typed))
blocks.caption: The identifier-confusion bug class in miniature: one signature over an untyped string is accepted for a different purpose. The fix labels what is being signed. Toy, not for production.

typed labels | device vouch accepted as identity-key vouch: False

blocks.md: **Threema** is a Swiss messenger. In January 2023 Kenneth Paterson, Matteo Scarlata and Kien Tuong Truong (ETH Zürich, Applied Cryptography Group) presented seven attacks in three threat models (network attacker, compromised server, compelled access to an unlocked phone). Examples: one compromised client ephemeral key let an attacker impersonate that client to the server "forever"; a **vouch box** forgery used a cross-protocol interaction between the client-to-server protocol and the E2E protocol; a malicious server could reorder and delete messages undetected because timestamps were not integrity-protected; the **Kompromat** attack abused one long-term key being used for both registration and E2E messages, so a malicious server could make a user unwittingly encrypt a message of the server's choosing to another user; and Threema ID export allowed cloning an account from an unlocked phone in seconds. Threema released a new protocol, Ibex, in November 2022 to add forward security; the researchers believed all their findings were mitigated but had not audited Ibex.

blocks.title: Matrix 2022: from small server powers to a full confidentiality break

nodes.label: Victim backs up to attacker key

scenes.caption: Start: a malicious homeserver, with every user and device verified, the strongest Matrix setting.
Design gap: the homeserver adds a member or device to the room. Clients share Megolm keys with it. Confidentiality broken.
Implementation gaps: forwarded keys accepted from anyone, then a Megolm/Olm protocol confusion upgrades them to fully trusted. Impersonation.
Chained: the attacker answers a new device's request for the backup key with its own key, and the homeserver can decrypt the backed-up Megolm sessions.
Fixes: authenticate room membership changes, domain-separate identifiers, accept keys only over verified Olm channels, check authenticity at decryption time, MAC the IV.

blocks.md: The Threema authors' lessons apply to every messenger: good libraries do not make a good protocol ("don't roll your own cryptographic protocol"), beware cross-protocol interactions and use separate keys for separate purposes, and analyse a design formally before release rather than patching after breaks.

Defender view for anyone running Matrix or a similar federated service: your homeserver is in the threat model of your own users. Keep clients updated (most fixes were client-side), enable settings that refuse to send to unverified devices, and treat unexpected device or member additions in sensitive rooms as alerts.

blocks.question: Why did Element showing "Mallory joined the room" not count as a fix for the membership attack?
options: Membership was still unauthenticated server data; in big rooms a join event goes unnoticed while clients send keys to the new member
blocks.explain: Detection by humans reading timelines does not scale. The keys flowed as soon as the server said Mallory was a member; the fix must stop that cryptographically.

blocks.question: The Threema Kompromat attack and the Matrix identifier confusion share which root cause?
options: A key or signature valid in one context was accepted in another: no key separation or domain separation
blocks.explain: Kompromat reused one key across registration and E2E messages; Matrix let one signature serve for device IDs and key IDs. Separate keys per purpose and typed labels in every signed or MACed input prevent both.

lessons.title: Telegram's MTProto, and why messengers need proofs

blocks.md: **Telegram** uses its own protocol, **MTProto**, instead of TLS between clients and servers. Default chats and all group chats are protected only by that client-to-server layer, so Telegram's servers can read them; end-to-end encrypted "secret chats" are "only optional and not available for group chats", as the analysis by Martin Albrecht, Lenka Mareková, Kenneth Paterson and Igors Stepanovs puts it ("Four Attacks and a Proof for Telegram", IEEE S&P 2022). Disclosed to Telegram on 16 April 2021:

1. A network attacker could **reorder messages** from client to server (their example turns "yes to pizzas, no to crimes" around).
2. An attacker could tell which of two special messages was encrypted, via resending of acknowledgements (theoretical).
3. Client code on Android, iOS and Desktop could in principle leak plaintext through timing, needing millions of messages: "almost impossible to carry out in practice".
4. An attacker-in-the-middle on the initial key negotiation, needing billions of messages within minutes.

Telegram fixed these, and the authors proved MTProto secure *with their changes*, under unusual assumptions on its building blocks.

blocks.code:
# Toy, not for production: authenticated encryption alone does not fix ORDER.
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
key = AESGCM(AESGCM.generate_key(128))
msgs = [b"I say yes to", b"all the pizzas", b"I say no to", b"all the crimes"]

def seal(i, m, with_counter):
    n = os.urandom(12)
    ad = i.to_bytes(8, "big") if with_counter else b""
    return i, n, key.encrypt(n, m, ad)

for with_counter in (False, True):
    wire = [seal(i, m, with_counter) for i, m in enumerate(msgs)]
    wire[1], wire[3] = wire[3], wire[1]          # the network swaps two messages
    expected, shown = 0, []
    for _, n, ct in wire:
        ad = expected.to_bytes(8, "big") if with_counter else b""
        try:
            shown.append(key.decrypt(n, ct, ad).decode())
            expected += 1
        except InvalidTag:
            shown.append("<rejected: out of order>")
            break
    print("counter in AD" if with_counter else "no counter   ", "|", " / ".join(shown))
blocks.caption: Authenticated encryption alone does not stop reordering. Binding a sequence number into the associated data does. Toy, not for production; real protocols buffer or reject depending on the transport.

blocks.code:
no counter    | I say yes to / all the crimes / I say no to / all the pizzas
counter in AD | I say yes to / <rejected: out of order>
blocks.caption: Output when run. Each message is individually authentic, but their order is not.

blocks.title: Analyses of messaging protocols, and what each found

scenes.caption: 2016 to 2017: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Dowling, Garratt and Stebila prove the security of Signal's key exchange core (X3DH plus Double Ratchet), with no major flaws found.
2018: Rösler, Mainka and Schwenk: group closeness and integrity not end-to-end protected in Signal, WhatsApp and Threema groups.
2021 to 2023: Telegram (4 attacks, then a proof of the fixed protocol), Matrix (practical breaks), Threema (7 attacks).
2023 to 2025: proofs arrive before or with deployment: PQXDH (ProVerif and CryptoVerif), iMessage PQ3 (Tamarin and a game-based proof), and SPQR with its own security proofs.

blocks.md:
**What a proof buys.** The Telegram authors' "somewhat opinionated" discussion defends the advice "don't roll your own crypto": standard protocols come with a proof that roughly says no adversary with stated capabilities can break stated goals unless a primitive is weak, which "significantly reduces the risk of catastrophic failure". Machine-checked tools make that routine: **ProVerif** works in a symbolic model and "is very efficient and fully automated"; **CryptoVerif** follows computational proof techniques under assumptions like IND-CCA; **Tamarin** was used for PQ3.

Proofs have limits. They cover the model, not the code, and the Matrix and Telegram client bugs were in implementations. They are a floor, not a ceiling.

Common misconception: "Telegram is encrypted, so it is like Signal". By default it is client-to-server encryption, like TLS to a web service: the provider can read cloud chats and all groups. Only optional one-to-one secret chats are end to end.

blocks.question: Every message in a protocol is protected by AES-GCM. Why could a network attacker still change the meaning of a conversation?
options: Nothing binds each message to its position, so reordering valid ciphertexts goes undetected
blocks.explain: Authenticity is per message. Order needs a counter or transcript hash inside the authenticated data, as in the fixed toy, the Double Ratchet's message numbers, or MLS's transcript hash.

blocks.question: A vendor says its new messenger protocol is secure because it uses only libsodium primitives. What is the strongest response?
options: Ask which AES key size it uses
Secure primitives do not make a secure protocol; ask for a published specification and a security analysis, ideally machine-checked, of the protocol itself
Accept it; libraries cannot be misused
blocks.explain: Threema used NaCl (a well-reviewed crypto library; libsodium is its fork) and Telegram used standard primitives; the breaks were in how they were composed. The Threema authors extend the mantra to "don't roll your own cryptographic protocol".

lessons.title: Operational failures: Signalgate and the TeleMessage archive (2025)

blocks.md:
Strong protocols do not stop people from adding the wrong person, using an unapproved app, or running a modified client. Two linked cases from 2025 show each failure.

**Signalgate (2025).** Senior US officials discussed airstrikes on Houthi forces in Yemen in a Signal group chat that also included Jeffrey Goldberg, editor-in-chief of The Atlantic, who reported it. After it became public, the Senate Armed Services Committee asked the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General (DoD OIG) on 26 March 2025 to review it.

In December 2025 the OIG released two reports. As reported by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/12/04/dod_hegseth_broke_pentagon_policy_signal/), the first (DODIG-2026-021) found the messages repeated material from a US Central Command email marked SECRET//NOFORN (classified Secret, not releasable to foreign nationals), and that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth did not comply with DoD rules by using a personal device and a non-approved commercial messaging app, risking "potential compromise of sensitive DoD information". It made no recommendation about the Secretary's use because this was "only one instance of a larger, DoD-wide issue", asking Central Command only to review its classification procedures. The [second (DODIG-2026-022)](https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/documents/reports/2025-12/DODIG_2026_022%20-%20Final_Redacted%20SECURE.pdf) summarised seven earlier OIG reports from 2021 to 2024 on unapproved messaging.

Notice what Signal did and did not do. The encryption worked; nobody broke a key. The failure was **membership** (a journalist was in the group), **policy** (classified material on an unapproved app and personal phones, where Signal itself was not the approved system for that information) and **records** (government records-retention rules versus disappearing messages, a setting that deletes messages from every device after a chosen time).

**TeleMessage (May 2025).** 404 Media reported that a Reuters photo showed Mike Waltz, a senior official who had been in that group chat, using **TM SGNL**, a modified Signal client from TeleMessage that archives copies of messages for record keeping. Security researcher and journalist Micah Lee analysed its published Android source and found that its archive server received **plaintext** chat logs. The [NVD entry for CVE-2025-47729](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-47729) states the archiving backend "holds cleartext copies of messages", unlike the vendor's "End-to-End encryption from the mobile phone through to the corporate archive" claim, "as exploited in the wild in May 2025". A second flaw, [CVE-2025-48927](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-48927), exposed a heap dump endpoint (`/heapdump`) of Spring Boot Actuator, a Java framework's management add-on, so attackers could download memory with messages. CISA added CVE-2025-47729 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 12 May 2025 and CVE-2025-48927 on 1 July 2025.

blocks.title: TM SGNL: a client that adds a third end

scenes.caption: TM SGNL registers with the real Signal service and interoperates, so a Signal user cannot tell a contact is running it.
After decrypting, the modified client copies every message to TeleMessage's archive server: plaintext leaves the endpoint.
The archive server exposed a heap dump URL. Memory snapshots contained chat content and credentials, and were downloaded by attackers.
Defence: approved, audited archiving designs; inventory of which clients are allowed; and the knowledge that any participant's client is an end you do not control.

blocks.md: E2EE protects the channel between ends. It cannot decide who the ends are (group membership), what an end does with plaintext (archiving clients, screenshots, backups), or whether that channel is the right one for the information (classification and records policy).

Defender view for organisations: publish which messaging apps are approved for which data, manage them on enrolled devices, audit group membership for sensitive rooms, decide retention deliberately (legal records rules can conflict with disappearing messages), and run archiving through vetted designs. Detection: mobile device management inventories reveal unapproved or modified clients; CISA's KEV listing is a prompt to hunt for TeleMessage use.

blocks.question: In Signalgate, which security property of Signal failed?
options: None of the cryptographic ones; an unintended participant was in the group and the app was used outside policy
blocks.explain: The journalist received messages because they were a member. Encryption delivered to every member exactly as designed; the failures were membership and policy, per the OIG findings.

blocks.question: You use real Signal; your contact uses TM SGNL. Where can your messages to them end up in plaintext?
options: Nowhere; your app encrypts end to end
On TeleMessage's archive server, because the contact's modified client copies decrypted messages there
blocks.explain: Encryption ends at the recipient's device, and that device's client forwarded plaintext to an archive. Micah Lee also notes Signal users cannot tell when a contact runs TM SGNL.

lessons.title: Lawful access and client-side scanning

blocks.md: Governments argue that E2EE hides serious crime, especially child sexual abuse material (CSAM), from investigators. Since E2EE leaves no server-side plaintext, proposals moved to the endpoint: **client-side scanning** (CSS), analysing content on the device before encryption or after decryption. A 2021 report by Hal Abelson and 13 coauthors (security and cryptography researchers including Ross Anderson, Whitfield Diffie and Bruce Schneier), ["Bugs in our Pockets: The Risks of Client-Side Scanning"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07450), describes the pitch: instead of weakening encryption or giving police backdoor keys, CSS "would enable on-device analysis of data in the clear" and report matches. Their conclusion: CSS "neither guarantees efficacious crime prevention nor prevents surveillance" and "creates serious security and privacy risks for all society".

blocks.title: Where client-side scanning sits

scenes.caption: Normal E2EE: the plaintext exists only inside the two devices.
CSS adds a matcher before encryption, with a database of target fingerprints supplied from outside. A match sends a report off the device.
The new risks: whoever controls the database controls what is searched for; the matcher can be fooled into false matches or misses; and every device now runs a reporting channel.

blocks.md: **Apple, 2021 to 2022.** In August 2021 Apple announced a plan to scan photos stored in iCloud for CSAM on the device, matching against known images. A perceptual hash called **NeuralHash** (a hash designed so that similar-looking images give the same value, unlike a cryptographic hash) did the matching. [Lukas Struppek and coauthors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06628) showed that "an adversary can manipulate the hash values by applying slight changes in images", "forcing or preventing hash collisions", which permits "from hiding abusive material to framing innocent users". Apple paused in September 2021 and told [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/apple-photo-scanning-csam-communication-safety-messages/) in December 2022 that the CSAM-detection tool for iCloud Photos was dead, focusing instead on opt-in Communication Safety features.

**UK, Online Safety Act 2023, [section 121](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/50/section/121).** Ofcom (the UK communications regulator) may, if it considers it "necessary and proportionate", give a provider a notice requiring it to "use accredited technology to identify CSEA content, whether communicated publicly or privately" (CSEA: child sexual exploitation and abuse), or to use "best endeavours to develop or source" such technology. For an E2EE service, identifying privately communicated content implies scanning at the endpoint. Separately, as lesson 17 showed, Apple withdrew Advanced Data Protection for new UK users. Access mechanisms become targets themselves: in 2024 the FBI and CISA [said](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/joint-statement-fbi-and-cisa-peoples-republic-china-prc-targeting-commercial-telecommunications) PRC actors inside US telecom networks copied information "subject to U.S. law enforcement requests pursuant to court orders".

**EU.** The Commission's May 2022 proposal for a regulation to combat child sexual abuse online included mandatory **detection orders**, criticised for applying to E2EE services. On 26 November 2025 the Council [adopted a position](https://eucrim.eu/news/csa-regulation-council-position-reached/) without mandatory detection orders, making the existing voluntary scanning regime permanent instead. Trilogue negotiations (three-way talks between Commission, Council and Parliament) started on 9 December 2025; a [Council note](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-9139-2026-INIT/en/pdf) records the fourth on 11 May 2026. Meanwhile the interim rule allowing voluntary scanning lapsed on 3 April 2026 after Parliament rejected an extension, then was [reinstated](https://eucrim.eu/news/interim-rules-on-voluntary-csam-detection-reinstated-until-2028/) by Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 until 3 April 2028. Check the current text before relying on any detail.

Mathematically there is no way to let a third party inspect E2EE content "only for bad content": either something outside the two ends learns about plaintext, or it does not. Every proposal moves that knowledge somewhere (a key escrow, a scanner, a backup), and that place becomes the new target.

blocks.question: A proposal says scanning happens "on the device, so encryption is not weakened". What is the strongest technical objection?
options: The plaintext is analysed and results leave the device, so whoever controls the matcher or its database gains a surveillance channel, and the matcher can be fooled
blocks.explain: The cipher is untouched, but the end is no longer private. Bugs in our Pockets argues CSS neither guarantees crime prevention nor prevents surveillance, and NeuralHash research showed collisions can be forced or avoided.

blocks.question: Why does a NeuralHash-style perceptual hash behave differently from SHA-256 for this purpose?
options: It is designed so similar images collide, which makes deliberate collisions and evasions possible with small image changes
It is computed on the server
blocks.explain: A cryptographic hash changes completely on any change, so it only finds exact copies. A perceptual hash tolerates changes by design, and Struppek et al. showed slight changes can force or prevent matches.

lessons.title: Reviewing a secure messenger, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Put the course together as questions to ask of any messaging product, protocol or deployment:

1. **Ends**: where is plaintext? Which clients (including modified or archiving ones) and devices are ends?
2. **First key**: X3DH, PQXDH or MLS KeyPackages? Are signatures checked before use, one-time keys deleted, encodings typed?
3. **Ongoing keys**: forward secrecy and post-compromise security? Bounds on skipped keys? Post-quantum rekeying (SPQR, PQ3)?
4. **Who is who**: safety numbers or codes, key-change warnings, key transparency with self-monitoring?
5. **Who is in**: are group and device membership changes authenticated, or does the server decide?
6. **Metadata**: what does the server log; sealed sender or equivalent; private groups; what timing leaks remain?
7. **Copies**: backups on by default? Who holds the key? Attempt limits?
8. **Assurance**: published specification, formal analysis, independent audits, a disclosure record.

blocks.title: One review, eight questions, mapped to the course

scenes.caption: Keys: questions 2 and 3, the handshake and the ratchets (lessons 2 to 9).
Identity and membership: questions 4 and 5 (lessons 10, 11, 13 to 16). Most real breaks lived here.
Around the protocol: questions 1, 6 and 7, the ends, metadata and copies (lessons 1, 12, 17, 20).
Assurance, question 8: proofs, audits and how past breaks were handled (lessons 5, 18, 19).

blocks.code:
# A review note template (fill one per product or deployment)
product: "<name and version>"

blocks.md:
**Practise legally.** Everything in this course can be explored without touching anyone else's messages:

- Re-run and extend the toy protocols here in a scratch venv; for example, add header encryption to the toy ratchet or a Remove operation to the toy tree.
- [CryptoHack](https://cryptohack.org/) has free challenges on Diffie-Hellman, elliptic curves and AES misuse.
- [The Cryptopals crypto challenges](https://cryptopals.com/) walk through breaking misused primitives such as repeated-key XOR and CTR nonce reuse, the bug in lesson 6.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/), the free practice platform that picoCTF now points learners to.
- Read the [Signal specifications](https://signal.org/docs/) and RFC 9420 alongside open-source implementations, and test only on your own accounts and devices: intercepting or decrypting other people's messages is illegal in most countries.

A secure messenger is a protocol plus a key directory plus a membership system plus clients plus backups plus people. The cryptography of the best-known protocols is strong and analysed; the failures in this course were nearly all at the joints.

blocks.question: A messenger uses the Signal protocol for content but lets its server add devices to accounts silently. Which review question exposes the risk?
options: 5, who is in (device and group membership)
blocks.explain: Server-controlled device lists let the server enrol a reader, as in the Matrix device attack and linked-device phishing. The handshake and ratchet are fine; membership is not authenticated.

blocks.question: Which finding is the most serious for a high-risk user population?
options: The app uses AES-256 instead of AES-128
Message history is backed up by default to a cloud where the provider holds the key
blocks.explain: A provider-held backup key recreates everything E2EE removed, for the whole history at once. The others are neutral or positive.
